prize_parts.citation: for realising and imaging strongly correlated many-body quantum systems with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, and for the theoretical proposals that made them controllable quantum simulators

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B012 as my preferred configuration, with Zoller for the theory and Bloch and Greiner for the experiments. The chair asks whether the same maturity standard is applied to every candidate, and I think B012 passes it most plainly: the Jaksch-Zoller proposal (1998), the Greiner-Bloch observation of the superfluid to Mott insulator transition (2002) and single-site-resolved quantum gas microscopy are about two decades old, reproduced by many groups and species, and checked quantitatively against Hubbard-type theory, so no part of the claim depends on an unsettled mechanism. The physics is clear in one sentence: a Hamiltonian that condensed-matter theory had only written down was built in the laboratory, with tunable interaction, geometry and dimension, and its quantum phase transition and correlations were imaged directly. It was the only shortlisted candidate that all eight members ranked in the opening round, and it is named as an alternative by Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Eriksson, which tells me the scientific case is not contested even if nobody else leads with it. I treat that as a weak observation and not as a vote count. The citation can also be made distinct from 2001 (condensation of dilute gases) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems): the new element is many-body strongly correlated matter with engineered Hamiltonians and single-site imaging, not condensation or single-particle control.
statement.case_against: The credit remains the weakest part. Four names are supplied for three places, Cirac is left out of my configuration, Jaksch co-authored the original proposal and is not on the supplied list, and Haensch, Esslinger and Bakr have arguable claims on the Mott and microscope results; I cannot claim the Zoller choice is airtight, only that the Jaksch-Zoller proposal is what the experiments implemented. The distance from the 2001 and 2012 prizes is a matter of careful wording and some members will find it too thin. The analogue-simulation payoff over classical methods has not been shown, so the prize would reward demonstrated many-body physics and not a solved computational problem. I am also now the only member with this configuration, and I should say plainly that on opening ballots B009 and B049 were broader in support; a committee that weights scientific clarity of the credit chain above maturity could reasonably choose B009, and one that weights maturity and clean attribution could choose B049.

responses.point: Eva argues that B049 has independent confirmation across many laboratories, a clean Katori-Ye credit, and that waiting for the redefinition of the second would reward administrative timing; she also concedes that the fundamental-physics results so far are null tests.
responses.response: I accept her point that a measurement prize does not need a new particle, and that the millimetre-scale redshift measurements are a real observation. My doubt is about what is being credited: the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 performance are decisive improvements in a measurement lineage that 2005 and 2012 already recognised, whereas B012 gives a new regime of matter. I agree with her that we should not wait for a formal redefinition of the second, and by the same token I do not think B012 should be penalised because analogue quantum advantage has not arrived. On her own standard, B049 is my second alternative, ahead of B040 and behind B009, and I would accept it if the committee wants the cleanest credit.

responses.point: Ulf keeps B009 first for the quantitative Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by the 2018 observation, concedes that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto antecedent needs handling in the citation, and ranks B040 below candidates without overlap with 2025.
responses.response: I agree with him on B040: I will not argue for it this year and he has seen that I withdrew it. On B009 my reservation is not the chain, which I find admirable, but the unequal maturity standard. He and Mehlig say a discovery does not need a settled mechanism, and that is fair if the citation names the flat bands and the observed correlated states and nothing about pairing; I would not object to that wording. But eight years against two decades is a real difference in how well the claim has been tested, so for me B009 is a strong first alternative and not the lead. If the committee decides to go with B009, the citation must be drafted to survive the earlier moire theory, and I would want the Lopes dos Santos et al. work addressed in the text.

responses.point: Olle ranks B009 first and B012 seventh in the opening ballot, values lattice simulators as tests of model Hamiltonians but says the practical advantage over classical simulation is unshown and the credit among Zoller, Jaksch, Cirac, Bloch and Greiner is unclear; in round 1 he lists B012 as a third alternative.
responses.response: I am glad that B012 stays among his alternatives, and I take his remaining worry about credit seriously. I would put the choice this way: Bloch and Greiner are the decisive experimentalists on the Mott transition and imaging, and for theory the Jaksch-Zoller proposal is the one that told experimentalists what to do, which is why I choose Zoller over Cirac. If the committee prefers Cirac, I would need to see an argument that his contribution to the lattice proposals was decisive for the experiments and not for the later quantum-information framing. On classical advantage, I still say the prize rewards demonstrated physics; the direct checks against Hubbard-type theory are exactly that.

responses.point: Eva ranks B009 first, rests the case on the testable prediction and on the moire structure and disorder being imaged directly, and names B012 and B049 as the more mature options if the committee decides to wait; she also notes that she and I share Chalmers.
responses.response: Her point that the experimental material can be characterised directly is a good one and strengthens B009, and her willingness to name B012 as a fallback is useful to me. I agree that the shared Chalmers connection matters only if B040 becomes a deciding candidate, and I do not believe it affects how we judge B012, B009 or B049. Where we still differ is timing: she and I both worry that disorder and strain are not yet under control in twisted graphene, and if that is a reason to wait for B009, it is a reason that favours B012, which has no such gap.

responses.point: Stefan puts B049 first, lists B012 as his first alternative, and in round 1 disclosed overlap of his quantum-memory collaborations with the Cirac and Zoller community and his involvement in WACQT.
responses.response: I am grateful for B012 as his first alternative. Given his overlap with the Cirac and Zoller community, I would suggest he be transparent on whether that bears on his view of the theory name, and I want it noted that I do not read it as a reason to discount his support. I also have a link to WACQT and I disclose that in the other direction, since it is a superconducting-circuit programme and has no documented relationship to the lattice experiments. On B049 I agree that the Katori-Ye split is clean and the Hall connection he raised looks to me like a proximity of environment rather than collaboration; that is for him and the chair to settle.

uncertainties: Whether Zoller or Cirac is the right theory name, and how to treat Jaksch and the early Mott-insulator and microscope contributors outside the supplied list.
Whether a citation can be written so that B012 is clearly distinct from the 2001 condensation and 2012 quantum-control prizes.
Whether the committee will apply the same maturity standard to B009 and B012, or accept that the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene can remain open.
Whether the committee prefers the Mott-insulator and microscope experiments or the theory proposal as the centre of the prize.
statement.conflict_note: I work in circuit and waveguide QED, direct WACQT at Chalmers, and have Chalmers colleagues (Per Delsing, C. M. Wilson) and a frequent co-author (Anton Frisk Kockum) in that community; Chalmers also hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. This matters for B040 (circuit QED), which I have withdrawn and would not argue for, and I would recuse myself from any decision on it. Olsson and I share Chalmers. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B012, B009 or B049.
